title: Envy and kindness
hook: envy sours another's good; kindness enjoys it

segments.voice: Yesterday, pride and humility. Your line was see yourself truly. Who did you ask for help, and how did it go? Day one thousand two hundred two.

The army is coming home. A young shepherd named David has just killed the giant, and the king, Saul, comes home with him. Women come out dancing with tambourines, and they sing a little song, the kind of thing a crowd chants. In the King James words: "Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands." A catchy line, and the text gives no sign anyone meant harm by it. But the next verse says Saul "was very wroth, and the saying displeased him." And then one short sentence: "Saul eyed David from that day and forward." Nothing bad had happened to Saul. He'd won. Someone else had simply won more. Today: envy and kindness.

Envy is a strange sin, because it doesn't even get you anything. Greed wants the thing. Envy can't stand that someone else has it. Thomas Aquinas, the medieval teacher, described it as sorrow over another person's good. Their good news lands in you as bad news. And the old Christian lists of deadly sins name envy among them. Proverbs puts it in the body: "envy the rottenness of the bones." It eats from the inside, and the other person often never knows. Now look who else is standing in that story. Saul's son, Jonathan. If anyone had reason to envy David, it was Jonathan. He was the king's son, next in line. David was the rival for his own future. And yet the text says "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Jonathan takes off his own robe and gives it to David, and his sword, and his bow. Later, when Saul is hunting David, Jonathan finds him in the wilderness and says, "thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee." Father and son, the same news, two opposite hearts. Saul watched David rise and saw a threat. Jonathan watched David rise and was glad. That gladness is what Christians mean by kindness here: not just being nice, but being able to enjoy someone else's good. Paul puts it in a single line to the church in Rome: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." For some, the weeping is the easier half. Sitting with a friend's bad news can come naturally. Celebrating a friend's promotion, the one you wanted, takes something else. That's the cure the tradition offers for envy: not pretending to want less, but practicing being glad.

Here's the practice: congratulate someone. Settle, and breathe. Choose one person whose good news reached you lately. A new job, a new baby, a trip, a win. Now draft the message in your head, the one you'll actually send. Keep it about them. No "but", no story about yourself, no comparing. Just their good thing, named, and your gladness at it. Try it a second time, shorter and warmer. If you pray, you can say Paul's line quietly: rejoice with them that do rejoice. When the bell rings, send it. The bell holds the time.
Envy and kindness. Envy is sorrow at another's good; kindness, in Jonathan's way, is gladness at it.
Your line: their joy is mine. Today, when someone's good news gives you a small sting, say it to yourself, and then say congratulations out loud. Day one thousand two hundred two.

howItsDone: Christian teaching on the deadly sins pairs envy with a virtue that answers it, often named kindness or charity, and some preachers point to Jonathan's friendship with David and Paul's call to rejoice with those who rejoice.

myth: envy is just another word for wanting what someone has
wanting the thing is greed. Aquinas described envy as sorrow at another's good: it can't stand that they have it.
Jonathan, the king's son, gave David his robe, sword and bow
the one with the most to lose was the one who was glad.
Saul turned against David because David harmed him
it began with a song. Saul had won too; David had simply won more.

fork.setup: you're Jonathan, the king's son. everyone is singing about David, the young man who may take the throne that would have been yours. what do you do?
options: keep your distance and watch him.
give him your robe, your sword and your bow.
tell your father he's a danger.
fork.reveal: Jonathan strips off his own robe and gives it to David, with his sword and bow. later he tells him: "thou shalt be king over Israel, and I shall be next unto thee."

original.note: Greek: envy, ill will at another's good. The word behind envy in the New Testament's lists of sins.

trapdoor: what you thought: envy means wanting nice things.
what it means: envy is the sting at someone else's good. Saul eyed David; Jonathan, with more to lose, was glad for him.
what a scholar hears: Aquinas's definition, sorrow at another's good, and Paul's answer to it: rejoice with them that do rejoice.
recall: gathering in silence, waiting on God
